e-566.knowledge_point: Determining the Position of a Particle Given Its Velocity and Initial Position
e-566.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t) = 2t+3t^2,$ where $t\geq 0$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=1$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
e-566.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t+3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}+{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(0) = 1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =(0)^{2}+(0)^{3}+C \\ C & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
x(t) = t^3+t^2+1.
$$

e-567.knowledge_point: Determining the Position of a Particle Given Its Acceleration, Initial Velocity and Initial Position
e-567.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t) = 1-2t,$ where $t\geq 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=1$ and velocity $v=2$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t >0.$
e-567.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1) = 2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =(1)-(1)^{2}+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t) = t-t^2 + 2.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (t-{t}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}+2t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(1) = 1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}-\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}+2(1)+K \\ K & =-\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t) = \dfrac{1}{2}t^2-\dfrac{1}{3}t^3 +2t -\dfrac{7}{6}.
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with velocity $v(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),$ where $t$ is the time. If the particle is at the position $x=3$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
after.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(0))+C \\ 3 & =-\frac{1}{2}+C \\ C & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
x(t)=\frac{7}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

Question 8

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration a(t)=6t+9t2, where t≥0 is the time. If the particle has position x=2 and velocity v=6 when t=1, calculate the position x of the particle at time t>0.

a
x(t)=t3+34t4+14
b
x(t)=t3+32t4−12
c
x(t)=3t3+34t4−74
d
x(t)=3t3+14t4−54
e
x(t)=t3+12t4+12
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating acceleration gives v(t)=3t²+3t³+C. Since v(1)=6, C=0. Integrating again gives x(t)=t³+(3/4)t⁴+K. Using x(1)=2 yields K=1/4, so option a is correct.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=6t+9{t}^{2}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=2$ and velocity $v=6$ when $t=1$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
after.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t+9{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=6.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =3(1)^{2}+3(1)^{3}+C \\ 6 & =6+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(1)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =(1)^{3}+\frac{3}{4}(1)^{4}+K \\ 2 & =\frac{7}{4}+K \\ K & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)={t}^{3}+\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4}+\frac{1}{4}.
$$

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration a(t)=6t+9t2, where t≥0 is the time. If the particle has position x=2 and velocity v=6 when t=1, calculate the position x of the particle at time t>0.

a
x(t)=t3+34t4+14
b
x(t)=t3+32t4−12
c
x(t)=3t3+34t4−74
d
x(t)=3t3+14t4−54
e
x(t)=t3+12t4+12
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity v(t):

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫(6t+9t2)dt=3t2+3t3+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(1)=6. Substituting this into the above gives

6=3(1)2+3(1)3+C6=6+CC=0.

So the velocity is given by v(t)=3t2+3t3.

Now, we integrate the velocity to get x(t):

x(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫(3t2+3t3)dt=t3+34t4+K

To determine K, we use the fact that x(1)=2. Substituting this into the above gives

2=(1)3+34(1)4+K2=74+KK=14.

Therefore, the position x of the particle at time t is x(t)=t3+34t4+14.

content.knowledge_point: Determining the Position of a Particle Given Its Acceleration, Initial Velocity and Initial Position
content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=6t+9{t}^{2}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=2$ and velocity $v=6$ when $t=1$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
content.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t+9{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=6.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =3(1)^{2}+3(1)^{3}+C \\ 6 & =6+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(1)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =(1)^{3}+\frac{3}{4}(1)^{4}+K \\ 2 & =\frac{7}{4}+K \\ K & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)={t}^{3}+\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4}+\frac{1}{4}.
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=4{e}^{4t}$, where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=\frac{1}{2}$ and velocity $v=1$ when $t=0$, calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t>0.$
after.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 4{e}^{4t}\text{d}t \\  & ={e}^{4t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & ={e}^{4t}+C \\ 1 & ={e}^{4(0)}+C \\ 1 & =1+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)={e}^{4t}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int {e}^{4t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4t}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4t}+K \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4(0)}+K \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{4}+K \\ K & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4t}+\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{4t}+1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫4e4tdt=e4t+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=1. Substituting this into the above gives

1=e4t+C1=e4(0)+C1=1+CC=0.

So the velocity is given by v(t)=e4t.

Now, we integrate the velocity to get x(t):

x(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫e4tdt=14e4t+K

To determine K, we use the fact that x(0)=12. Substituting this into the above gives

12=14e4t+K12=14e4(0)+K12=14+KK=14.

Therefore, the position x of the particle at time t is x(t)=14e4t+14=e4t+14.

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\frac{1}{1}+C \\ C & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=-\frac{1}{t}+1.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-\frac{1}{t}+1)\text{d}t \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(1)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1+K \\ 4 & =-0+1+K \\ K & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t+3.
$$

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration a(t)=1t2, where t≥1 is the time. If the particle has position x=4 and velocity v=0 when t=1, calculate the position x of the particle at time t≥1.

a
x(t)=−ln⁡t+t+3
b
 x(t)=ln⁡t−2t+4
c
 x(t)=−ln⁡t+t+1
d
x(t)=−ln⁡t+2t
e
x(t)=ln⁡t+2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity v(t):

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫1t2dt=−1t+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(1)=0. Substituting this into the above gives

0=−11+CC=1.

So the velocity is given by v(t)=−1t+1.

Now, we integrate the velocity to get x(t):

x(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫(−1t+1)dt=−ln⁡t+t+K

To determine K, we use the fact that x(1)=4. Substituting this into the above gives

4=−ln⁡(1)+1+K4=−0+1+KK=3.

Therefore, the position x of the particle at time t is x(t)=−ln⁡t+t+3.

content.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},$ where $t\ge 1$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=4$ and velocity $v=0$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t\ge 1.$
content.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\frac{1}{1}+C \\ C & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=-\frac{1}{t}+1.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-\frac{1}{t}+1)\text{d}t \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(1)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1+K \\ 4 & =-0+1+K \\ K & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t+3.
$$
